content: Induced abortions are among the most frequently performed medical interventions globally. Over the past decade, various medical methods for abortion have been developed to complement existing surgical techniques. This review systematically analyzed evidence from randomized controlled trials that compared surgical and medical methods for terminating pregnancies during the first trimester. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy, side effects, and acceptability of medical methods in comparison to surgical methods for first-trimester abortions. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE (with a Cochrane 3-stage search strategy covering 1966-2000), and Popline (1970-2000). No language restrictions were applied during the search, and reference lists of relevant studies were reviewed. Additionally, experts from the World Health Organization's Human Reproduction Programme (WHO/HRP) were consulted. The review included randomized trials that compared any surgical abortion method with any medical abortion method during the first trimester. The quality of the trials was assessed, and data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers. Seven studies were included in the review, though most had small sample sizes. These studies compared four different medical interventions—prostaglandins alone, mifepristone alone, mifepristone combined with misoprostol, and methotrexate combined with misoprostol—against vacuum aspiration, a common surgical method. In some cases, the results were based on data from a single trial. When comparing prostaglandins alone to vacuum aspiration, the rate of incomplete abortions was significantly higher in the prostaglandin group (relative risk 2.7, 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 6.8). However, there were no data available in this review comparing the most commonly used medical method (mifepristone/misoprostol) with surgical abortion. The duration of bleeding was found to be longer in the medical abortion groups compared to those undergoing vacuum aspiration. Only one major complication, a case of uterine perforation, was reported in the surgical group across all trials. There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of ongoing pregnancies at follow-up or the incidence of pelvic infections. Unfortunately, no data were available in the review regarding the acceptability of the procedures, side effects, or women's satisfaction with the methods. The authors concluded that the findings were based on relatively small trials, which limits the strength of the evidence. Prostaglandins used alone appear to be less effective and more painful compared to surgical methods for first-trimester abortion. However, there is insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about the acceptability and side effects of medical versus surgical methods. Further research is needed to evaluate the efficacy of currently used methods and to better understand women's preferences and experiences.
